images.title: Daisy comes for lunch WAH 022 - Flickr - Stewart Black.jpg
images.author: Stewart Black
images.description:
The We're Here group are visiting Feeling Happy today. During a year in which my life feels like that of a man able to see into the future and yet forced to steer the Titanic on its maiden voyage, finding suitable subject matter wasn't easy. Or so I thought until Daisy came round for lunch. I like preparing food and I love sharing it with my lovely daughter and so this is what makes me happy.

Salad greens from our garden, char-grilled sweet potato slices, grilled and marinaded tofu, strawberries and tomatoes, tortilla wraps and chips and a vegan nacho cheese dip made from cashews and roasted bell pepper. Yum.

images.title: Aunt Edith's Banana Bread Recipe.jpg
images.author: Celeste Lindell
images.description:
Aunt Edith's Banana Bread
Stays moist a week
1/2 cup shortening or butter
1 cup white sugar
2 eggs
2 very ripe bananas
1 tsp. baking soda
1/2 tsp. salt
2 cups flour (no more)
1 cup chopped walnuts
Cream together shortening and sugar. Add eggs and mix well. Mash in bananas. Combine flour, baking soda and salt (cut back or eliminate salt if using salted butter instead of shortening) and mix into wet ingredients. Stir in walnuts. Bake in a well-greased loaf pan at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for 60-70 minutes or until top is very brown and any cracks in the top are fairly dry inside.

The original recipe had you prepare the loaf pan by greasing it, lining it with waxed paper and greasing the waxed paper. Then when the loaf was done, you removed it from the pan and peeled off the paper. At some point I just stopped doing that and began to grease the pan directly and the results have been fine. I don't really know why that seemed like a necessary step back in the day, but I merely mention it as a curiosity.

images.title: CSIRO ScienceImage 11385 Pasta made from durum wheat.jpg
images.author: division, CSIRO
images.description: CSIRO researchers have developed a salt tolerant durum wheat that yields 25 per cent more grain than the parent variety in saline soils. The breakthrough will enable wheat farmers to achieve higher yields of durum wheat in saline soils. Although durum wheat is less salt tolerant than bread wheat it attracts a premium price because of its superior pasta making qualities. The CSIRO Plant Industry research team responsible for the breakthrough isolated two salt tolerance genes (Nax1 and Nax2) derived from the old wheat relative Triticum monococcum. Both genes work by excluding  potentially toxic sodium from the leaves by limiting its passage from the roots to the shoots. Through traditional, non-GM breeding methods aided by molecular markers the team was able to introduce the salt exclusion genes into durum wheat lines.

images.title: Home made pizza (17156898368).jpg
images.author: N i c o l a from Fiumicino (Rome), Italy
images.description:
Pizza is an oven-baked flat bread generally topped with tomato sauce and cheese. It is commonly supplemented with a selection of meats, vegetables and condiments. The term was first recorded in AD 997, in a Latin manuscript from Gaeta in Lazio, Central Italy.[1] The modern pizza was invented in Naples, Italy, and the dish and its variants have since become popular in many areas of the world.[2]
In 2009, upon Italy's request, Neapolitan pizza was safeguarded in the European Union as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed dish.[3][4] The Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (the True Neapolitan Pizza Association) is a non-profit organization founded in 1984 with legal and operational headquarters in Naples. Its mission is to promote and protect the "true Neapolitan pizza" defined as the product made in accordance with the International Regulations for the brand.[5]

Pizza is sold fresh, frozen or in portions. Various types of ovens are used to cook them and many varieties exist. Several similar dishes are prepared from ingredients commonly used in pizza preparation, such as calzone and stromboli.

images.title: Pizza IMG 0793 (39443275275).jpg
images.author: N i c o l a from Fiumicino (Rome), Italy
images.description:
Pizza is a traditional Italian dish consisting of a yeasted flatbread typically topped with tomato sauce and cheese and baked in an oven. It can also be topped with additional vegetables, meats, and condiments, and can be made without cheese.
The term pizza was first recorded in the 10th century, in a Latin manuscript from the Southern Italy town of Gaeta in Lazio, on the border with Campania.[1] Modern pizza was invented in Naples, and the dish and its variants have since become popular and common in many areas of the world.[2] In 2009, upon Italy's request, Neapolitan pizza was registered with the European Union as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed dish.[3][4] Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (True Neapolitan Pizza Association), a non-profit organization founded in 1984 with headquarters in Naples, aims to "promote and protect... the true Neapolitan pizza".[5]
Pizza is one of the most popular foods in the world and common fast food item in Europe and North America. Many independent or chain restaurants, cafes, and fast food outlets offer pizza. Restaurants or chains specializing in pizza are pizzerias. Pizza delivery is common in some parts of the world.

Pizza is sold fresh or frozen, either whole or in portions.[6] Various types of ovens are used to cook them and many varieties exist. Several similar dishes are prepared from ingredients commonly used in pizza preparation, such as calzone and stromboli. In the United States, pizza is usually eaten out of hand after dividing into slices from a large pizza or small pizzetta as a whole. In Italy, pizza is eaten with a fork and knife in restaurants, but is also sold to take away and eaten out of hand. Frozen pizza became popular in the late 20th century.

images.title: Home made pizza (17156898368).jpg
images.author: N i c o l a from Fiumicino (Rome), Italy
images.description:
Pizza is an oven-baked flat bread generally topped with tomato sauce and cheese. It is commonly supplemented with a selection of meats, vegetables and condiments. The term was first recorded in AD 997, in a Latin manuscript from Gaeta in Lazio, Central Italy.[1] The modern pizza was invented in Naples, Italy, and the dish and its variants have since become popular in many areas of the world.[2]
In 2009, upon Italy's request, Neapolitan pizza was safeguarded in the European Union as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed dish.[3][4] The Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (the True Neapolitan Pizza Association) is a non-profit organization founded in 1984 with legal and operational headquarters in Naples. Its mission is to promote and protect the "true Neapolitan pizza" defined as the product made in accordance with the International Regulations for the brand.[5]

Pizza is sold fresh, frozen or in portions. Various types of ovens are used to cook them and many varieties exist. Several similar dishes are prepared from ingredients commonly used in pizza preparation, such as calzone and stromboli.

images.title: Pizza IMG 0793 (39443275275).jpg
images.author: N i c o l a from Fiumicino (Rome), Italy
images.description:
Pizza is a traditional Italian dish consisting of a yeasted flatbread typically topped with tomato sauce and cheese and baked in an oven. It can also be topped with additional vegetables, meats, and condiments, and can be made without cheese.
The term pizza was first recorded in the 10th century, in a Latin manuscript from the Southern Italy town of Gaeta in Lazio, on the border with Campania.[1] Modern pizza was invented in Naples, and the dish and its variants have since become popular and common in many areas of the world.[2] In 2009, upon Italy's request, Neapolitan pizza was registered with the European Union as a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed dish.[3][4] Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (True Neapolitan Pizza Association), a non-profit organization founded in 1984 with headquarters in Naples, aims to "promote and protect... the true Neapolitan pizza".[5]
Pizza is one of the most popular foods in the world and common fast food item in Europe and North America. Many independent or chain restaurants, cafes, and fast food outlets offer pizza. Restaurants or chains specializing in pizza are pizzerias. Pizza delivery is common in some parts of the world.

Pizza is sold fresh or frozen, either whole or in portions.[6] Various types of ovens are used to cook them and many varieties exist. Several similar dishes are prepared from ingredients commonly used in pizza preparation, such as calzone and stromboli. In the United States, pizza is usually eaten out of hand after dividing into slices from a large pizza or small pizzetta as a whole. In Italy, pizza is eaten with a fork and knife in restaurants, but is also sold to take away and eaten out of hand. Frozen pizza became popular in the late 20th century.

images.title: Pizze alla napoletana - Il Bersagliere 1880 (cropped).png
images.author: Unknown authorUnknown author
images.description:
“Pizze alla napoletana” (Neaplolitan pizza) – Article in the Roman newspaper Il Bersagliere of 19th June 1880, giving an account of Giovanni Brandi, owner of several Neapolitan pizzerias, who claims to have been invited to make pizzas (then a peasant food) for Queen Margherita of Italy and crown prince Victor Emmanuel.
(This is almost a decade earlier than the date given on the counterfeit document made out to Raffaele Esposito (Brandi’s son in law), which is still often cited as the origin of the Pizza Margherita. Compare Zachary Novak: Folklore, Fakelore, History: The Origins of the Pizza Margherita.)

images.title: Gnocchi al pesto - homemade.jpg
images.author: Fuerteadventours
images.description:
A matter of legacy: Pesto sauce.
One of the sweetest memories of my childhood, is the moment when I used to help my mother preparing Pesto sauce.
We left Genoa and we emigrated to a small village on the Swiss border, when I was just a little girl.
Preparing Pesto, for my mother and my family was something like going back home.
That’s why it was so important for my mother to make it only when, coming back after visiting my grandparents and uncles based in Genoa, we could bring home, like a trophy, the original Genoese basil: Prà basil.
This basil has a particular sensory quality, that makes Pesto a very special sauce: tasty, genuine and, above all, healthy.
Its essential oils make it magic and you can easily recognize it from the scent, the color and the shape of the leaves. Remember, if you want to live this mystic experience: small, light green leaves in the shape of a teaspoon!
So even now, when I’m going to make homemade Pesto, I blindly follow my mother’s law: “Don’t make Pesto, if you can get Prà basil!”.
Furthermore, basil is not the only issue, when one talk about traditional Pesto sauce.
This sauce is a matter of legacy. Even if the modern recipe is not so ancient, it dates back to the beginning of the 20th century, it preserves the echoes of ancient recipes and know-hows coming especially from the Romans and from the Arabs.
It is the case for garlic, a disinfectant, and for coarse salt, known for its preservative properties. It is the case of pine nuts, strictly coming from Pisa, and of the two traditional cheese, Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Sardo. But, it’s also a matter of the know-how and backstory behind marble mortar and pestle, the traditional tools used since the origin of this and other Ligurian sauces.
In my opinion there is nothing so impressive and evocative as to get intensely inside the traditional cuisine of a place, in order to deeply grasp the meaning of its history and its evolutions.
But now let me bring you inside the family recipe and some tips that my mother passed on to me.
Seven are the ingredients and seven are the steps and the tips that I’m going to give you, let’s start!
1)	First step and first ingredient: garlic, possibly organic and Italian (top choice: Aglio from Vessalico). Peel it and remove the germ from the garlic clove and start to beat it inside the mortar;
2)	Add Pisa pine nuts (25/30 gr.) and keep beating them into a pulp.
3)	Put in 1 teaspoon of coarse salt and mix it.
4)	And now comes the moment of “his majesty” - basil: the leaves of one small bunch for each guest; this is one of the most crucial moments. As I told you before, basil boats very delicate and healthy essential oils and it’s extremely important to preserve them. So if you use the mortar and the pestle the movement should be precise and quick. If you are using a food processor, it’s vital, first of all,  to keep the  blender jar in the freezer for about an hour. It’s mandatory not to over heat the basil. So please be careful.
5)	Now you can add Parmigiano Reggiano (about 65/70 gr of 18/24 months aged cheese) freshly grated.
6)	And then you can add Pecorino Sardo (about 30/35 gr of 10 months cheese) freshly grated too.
7)	At the and of this process of melting and beating, another key moment: EVO, best if Ligurian. The quantity depends on the consistence we want to obtain that could be a little bit different according to the kind of pasta that you are going to dress. But it also crucial to add the oil scantily, without stopping to mix the sauce	
And that’s it, folks! Very soon Pesto sauce will be ready and your guests will be delighted and in love with it. 
And remember… it’s a family secret! ;-)
Ps. 

leave a comment below, if you would like more information on the history of the pesto or on the recipes related to it

images.title: Качамак (бакрдан) со кисело млеко 01.jpg
images.author: Kotle31
images.description:
Kachamak (Macedonian: Качамак) is a traditional dish 
made of corn flour, potato and, sometimes, feta cheese. 
Similar to the Italian polenta, it is prepared by boiling the 
mixture thick or rare depending on taste, and then mashing 
while the pot is still on the fire. It is usually served with milk, 

plain Yogurt, sour cream or sometimes with bacon.

images.title: Polenta "uncia" servita al rifugio del Monte Palanzone "Rifugio Riella" (Como) - 08-11-2015.JPG
images.author: Mænsard vokser
images.description: Polenta served in the recipe called "uncia", in the dialect of Como, which means greasy. This version of polenta is called greasy because it is blended with cheese and butter until both of them melt and mixed with the porridge. This one was served at the alpine hut "Rifugio Riella" on the mountain Monte Palanzone (Como) on the 8th of november in 2015.

images.title: DFC 2103 Golden flaky croissant pockets filled with creamy chicken and corn finished with a sprig of parsley.jpg
images.author: PattayaPatrol
images.description: The photo shows a tray of freshly baked pastries that appear to be savory croissants or stuffed pastry puffs. They have a golden-brown, flaky exterior with a glossy finish, suggesting they've been egg-washed before baking. Each pastry is filled with what looks like a creamy mixture that might contain chicken or seafood, with small bits of corn visible in some of them. The pastries are garnished with small sprigs of fresh parsley on top, adding a touch of vibrant green color. They're arranged neatly on what appears to be a baking sheet or serving tray, likely ready to be served as appetizers or party snacks. These look like they could be chicken or seafood vol-au-vents or similar savory filled pastries that would be served at a gathering or buffet.

images.title: Homemade Panettone IMG 2506 (15459336634).jpg
images.author: N i c o l a from Fiumicino (Rome), Italy
images.description:
In the early 20th century, two enterprising Milanese bakers began to produce panettone in large quantities in the rest of Italy. In 1919, Angelo Motta started producing his eponymous brand of cakes. It was also Motta who revolutionised the traditional panettone by giving it its tall domed shape by making the dough rise three times, or almost 20 hours, before cooking, giving it its now-familiar light texture. The recipe was adapted shortly after by another baker, Gioacchino Alemagna, around 1925, who also gave his name to a popular brand that still exists today. The stiff competition between the two that then ensued led to industrial production of the cake-like bread. Nestlé took over the brands together in the late 1990s, but Bauli, an Italian bakery company based in Verona, has acquired Motta and Alemagna from Nestlé.
As a result of the fierce competition, by the end of World War II, panettone was cheap enough for anyone and soon became the country's leading Christmas sweet. Northern Italian immigrants to Argentina and Brazil also brought their love of panettone, and panettone is enjoyed for Christmas with hot cocoa or liquor during the holiday season, which became a mainstream tradition in those countries. In some places, it replaces the King cake.

images.title: Carl Griffith sourdough starter stiff just fed side.jpg
images.author: Anon423
images.description:
About 9 ounces of sourdough starter derived from Carl Griffith's 1847 Oregon Trail Sourdough sits in a plastic tub.
A sample of live starter cultures was received from the 1847 Oregon Trail Sourdough Preservation Society, also known as Carl's Friends, which maintains and shares the historic sourdough starter. This lineage has been continually cultivated since at least 1847 for making bread.
This picture was taken just after the starter was fed with fresh flour and water, at about a 3:2 ratio, so little fermentation has occurred.

The side of the container is labeled "Carl Griffith 1847".

images.author: Anon423
images.description: A small amount of sourdough starter, derived from Carl Griffith's 1847 Oregon Trail Sourdough, sits in a plastic tub. A sample of live starter cultures was received from the 1847 Oregon Trail Sourdough Preservation Society, also known as Carl's Friends, which maintains and shares the historic sourdough starter. images.title: Carl Griffith sourdough starter paste 8 hours.jpg
images.author: Anon423
images.description:
A small amount of sourdough starter, derived from Carl Griffith's 1847 Oregon Trail Sourdough, sits in a plastic tub.
A sample of live starter cultures was received from the 1847 Oregon Trail Sourdough Preservation Society, also known as Carl's Friends, which maintains and shares the historic sourdough starter. This lineage has been continually cultivated since at least 1847 for making bread.
This picture was taken about 8 hours after the starter was fed with fresh flour and water at a 1:1 ratio, and small bubbles have formed.

The side of the container is labeled "Carl Griffith 1847", visible in reverse through the transparent plastic.

images.title: DFC 3512 Juicy grilled steak topped with herb butter served with mashed potatoes fresh greens and a side of gravy.jpg
images.author: PattayaPatrol
images.description: This photo shows a beautifully plated steak dish served on a black plate. The steak appears to be grilled to medium or medium-rare and is topped with small dollops of herb butter that's melting over the meat. The steak is accompanied by what looks like mashed potatoes on the side. There's also a fresh side salad with green lettuce and shredded carrots, adding color and freshness to the plate. A small ramekin of sauce, possibly a gravy or steak sauce, is included on the plate. The entire dish is presented on what appears to be a textured placemat, giving it a restaurant-quality presentation. This looks like a classic steak dinner with traditional sides - a hearty and appealing meal.

images.title: DFC 2081 Juicy grilled steak topped with herb butter served with fries sautéed green beans coleslaw and a side of gravy.jpg
images.author: PattayaPatrol
images.description: This photo shows a hearty meal served on a white plate. The main feature is a steak topped with what appears to be a pat of herb butter or flavored compound butter. Surrounding the steak are several side dishes: a serving of french fries, some green beans (possibly sautéed with garlic or other seasonings), and a small portion of coleslaw or similar cabbage salad with a lettuce leaf. There's also a light blue gravy boat or sauce dish in the upper left containing what might be a sauce or gravy for the steak. The meal is presented on what looks like a wooden table, creating a casual dining atmosphere. This appears to be a classic steak dinner with traditional accompaniments.

images.title: Making vinaigrette.jpg
images.author: jeffreyw
images.description: Vinaigrette is a mixture (emulsion) of oils, such as soybean oil, canola oil, olive oil, corn oil, sunflower oil, safflower oil, peanut oil, grape seed oil, and vinegar, sometimes flavored with herbs, spices, and other ingredients. It is used most commonly as a salad dressing, but also as a cold sauce or marinade. Here, the process is beginning as a vegetable oil is added to vinegar and mustard. Mustard is often used as an emulsifier in vinaigrette.

images.title: Oyster with grilled mayo - Shira Nui AUD4.50 each (4760494410).jpg
images.author: Alpha from Melbourne, Australia
images.description:
Sweet, briney, tasty raw oysters with a dollop of mayonnaise grilled to a caramelly crust makes an incredible combination. The silky texture of the oyster is further enhanced by the creamy mayonnaise.
---
Dinner with Jennie and David, omakase-style at the sushi counter.
Shira Nui 不知火
247 Springvale Rd
Glen Waverley VIC 3150
(03) 9886-7755
Lunch Tue-Sat noon-2pm. Dinner Tue-Sun 6pm-10pm
Reviews:
- <a href="http://www.theage.com.au/news/restaurant-reviews/shira-nui/2007/05/22/1179601388220.html" rel="nofollow">Shira Nui, by Dani Valent, Epicure, The Age May 22, 2007</a> Sit at the sushi counter. Order the omakase
- <a href="http://www.theage.com.au/news/restaurant-reviews/shira-nui/2005/10/10/1128796455935.html" rel="nofollow">Shira Nui By Jane Faulkner, Epicure, The Age October 10, 2005</a> Shira Nui is worth crossing town for.
- <a href="http://www.theage.com.au/articles/2003/08/05/1059849389300.html" rel="nofollow">Fusion without power By John Lethlean, The Age August 5 2003</a> At Shira Nui, only certain types of sushi will be delivered to the table, so fanatical is the chef. The full range is available only to a manageable group of sushi-bar diners. He makes; you eat immediately; then he makes again. This is the omakase menu, a sushi-only degustation that is the purest, most pleasurable dining experience I have had all year.
- <a href="http://tummyrumbles.com/2009/05/shira-nuiagain.html" rel="nofollow">Shira Nui ... again - TummyRumbles by mellie on May 17th, 2009</a>

images.title: Teriyaki Salmon Claypot Rice - Claypot King, Glen Waverley (2993613849).jpg
images.author: Alpha from Melbourne, Australia
images.description:
Teriyaki Salmon Claypot Rice - Claypot King, Glen Waverley ~AUD10
---
Busy as ever on a Saturday evening.
The 梅菜扣肉煲 Belly Pork with Preserved Vegetable was pretty good, or so my mum says. With my clogged nose, it was... salty :)
Aunt Lay Leong though that it was probably because the pork was well marinated in 五香粉 five-spive powder, and the deep frying before stewing releases the flavours.
The salmon is a healthy option, very fresh and moist. Packed with good fats!
煲仔靓汤 Claypot King
72 Kingsway, Glen Waverley
03 9561 8884

My plan is to serve the grilled veggies on French bread with some herb mayonnaise and maybe a slice of cheese. If the recipe is as good as it looks, I'll post it tomorrow.

The recipe IS as good as it looks.

images.author: Alpha from Melbourne, Australia
images.description:
Bibimbap - Seoul Garden AUD8
---
The bibimbap was a bit bland despite adding gobs of doenjang spicy bean paste and kimchi. Perhaps it was the lack of a drizzle of sesame oil, or perhaps the strips of beef didn't seem to bear any grill-marks nor did it seem marinated.
It's a pity though, because the presentation was clean and the sliced vegetables were fresh and crunchy.
Seoul Garden Restaurant

images.title: 20160130 Sri Lanka 4311+15-18+20 Galle sRGB (25470298700).jpg
images.author: Dan Lundberg
images.description:
Our Farewell Dinner is outside on a terrace of our hotel as the sun sets over the Indian Ocean.  The starter is Coriander Seared Yellowfin Tuna and Lemon Dill Marinated Calamari on Green Papaya Relish with Vodka Orange Dressing and Salmon Rice (plus a little garnish of caviar).  The Southern Seafood Soup with Garlic Toast is followed by a Gin & Lemon Sorbet to clear the palate.  For my main course I choose Grilled Honey-Glazed Fillet of Pork with Port Wine Sauce & Mango Chutney with Baked Vegetables and Dauphinoise Potato.  My dessert selection is Tiramisu and Mango Basil Ice Cream with Mocha Froth and Red Fruit Sauce.

images.author: Takeaway
images.description:
A Roman style (very thin and slightly crispy) pizza "con funghi e olive": with mushrooms and (black) olives.
Toppings on this pizza are: sliced mushrooms, sliced black olives, mozzarella cheese and tomato sauce. I personally added some olive oil infused with dried chillies and garlic, freshly ground black pepper and some (I like spicy food) ground dried chillies. In the city of Chiang Mai, Thailand.

images.title: Liat Portal for Foodie Disorder - Salmon with peas garlic and jalapeño in Moroccan fish sauce.jpg
images.author: HaJunkiyada
images.description: Home-cooked salmon prepared in a pot, simmered with green peas, whole garlic cloves, sliced jalapeño, and herbs in a Moroccan fish sauce. images.title: Turkey breast in a paprika and tomato sauce.jpg
images.author: Rexipe Rexipe from London, UK
images.description:
Turkey Breast in Tomato & Paprika
www.rexipe.com/recipes/607-turkey_breast_in_tomato__paprika
Summary
This is a great healthy dish ... I like it in the summer with some wholemeal pitta bread, salad and yogurt 
Ingredients
4 Turkey Breast 
4 Tablespoons of Olive Oil 
2 crushed garlic cloves 
1 small chilli (chopped) 
1 small punnet of cherry tomatoes 
1/2 bunch of fresh coriander (chopped) 
4 Tablespoons of tomato puree 
1 teaspoon of paprika 
Method
Mix the olive oil, garlic and chilli to create a marinate 
Coat the Turkey breasts and leave overnight 
Take a dish and place the turkey breasts in the dish 
Mix the coriander, tomato puree and paprika, add some of the marinade to this mixture and stir well 
Coat the turkey breasts with the sauce above 
Place the cherry tomatoes around the turkey breasts 
Cook in the oven on 200C for around 30 minutes 
Cool and serve with wholemeal pitta bread, salad and yogurt 
To see more recipes like this please visit us as www.rexipe.com
Thanks
[1]
Faz

(Rexipe.com, London)

images.title: Pizza con funghi e olive chiang mai.jpg
images.author: Takeaway
images.description:
A Roman style (very thin and slightly crispy) pizza "con funghi e olive": with mushrooms and (black) olives.
Toppings on this pizza are: sliced mushrooms, sliced black olives, mozzarella cheese and tomato sauce. I personally added some olive oil infused with dried chillies and garlic, freshly ground black pepper and some (I like spicy food) ground dried chillies. In the city of Chiang Mai, Thailand.

images.title: Gnocchi al pesto - homemade.jpg
images.author: Fuerteadventours
images.description:
A matter of legacy: Pesto sauce.
One of the sweetest memories of my childhood, is the moment when I used to help my mother preparing Pesto sauce.
We left Genoa and we emigrated to a small village on the Swiss border, when I was just a little girl.
Preparing Pesto, for my mother and my family was something like going back home.
That’s why it was so important for my mother to make it only when, coming back after visiting my grandparents and uncles based in Genoa, we could bring home, like a trophy, the original Genoese basil: Prà basil.
This basil has a particular sensory quality, that makes Pesto a very special sauce: tasty, genuine and, above all, healthy.
Its essential oils make it magic and you can easily recognize it from the scent, the color and the shape of the leaves. Remember, if you want to live this mystic experience: small, light green leaves in the shape of a teaspoon!
So even now, when I’m going to make homemade Pesto, I blindly follow my mother’s law: “Don’t make Pesto, if you can get Prà basil!”.
Furthermore, basil is not the only issue, when one talk about traditional Pesto sauce.
This sauce is a matter of legacy. Even if the modern recipe is not so ancient, it dates back to the beginning of the 20th century, it preserves the echoes of ancient recipes and know-hows coming especially from the Romans and from the Arabs.
It is the case for garlic, a disinfectant, and for coarse salt, known for its preservative properties. It is the case of pine nuts, strictly coming from Pisa, and of the two traditional cheese, Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Sardo. But, it’s also a matter of the know-how and backstory behind marble mortar and pestle, the traditional tools used since the origin of this and other Ligurian sauces.
In my opinion there is nothing so impressive and evocative as to get intensely inside the traditional cuisine of a place, in order to deeply grasp the meaning of its history and its evolutions.
But now let me bring you inside the family recipe and some tips that my mother passed on to me.
Seven are the ingredients and seven are the steps and the tips that I’m going to give you, let’s start!
1)	First step and first ingredient: garlic, possibly organic and Italian (top choice: Aglio from Vessalico). Peel it and remove the germ from the garlic clove and start to beat it inside the mortar;
2)	Add Pisa pine nuts (25/30 gr.) and keep beating them into a pulp.
3)	Put in 1 teaspoon of coarse salt and mix it.
4)	And now comes the moment of “his majesty” - basil: the leaves of one small bunch for each guest; this is one of the most crucial moments. As I told you before, basil boats very delicate and healthy essential oils and it’s extremely important to preserve them. So if you use the mortar and the pestle the movement should be precise and quick. If you are using a food processor, it’s vital, first of all,  to keep the  blender jar in the freezer for about an hour. It’s mandatory not to over heat the basil. So please be careful.
5)	Now you can add Parmigiano Reggiano (about 65/70 gr of 18/24 months aged cheese) freshly grated.
6)	And then you can add Pecorino Sardo (about 30/35 gr of 10 months cheese) freshly grated too.
7)	At the and of this process of melting and beating, another key moment: EVO, best if Ligurian. The quantity depends on the consistence we want to obtain that could be a little bit different according to the kind of pasta that you are going to dress. But it also crucial to add the oil scantily, without stopping to mix the sauce	
And that’s it, folks! Very soon Pesto sauce will be ready and your guests will be delighted and in love with it. 
And remember… it’s a family secret! ;-)
Ps.

images.title: Gnocchi al pesto - homemade.jpg
images.author: Fuerteadventours
images.description:
A matter of legacy: Pesto sauce.
One of the sweetest memories of my childhood, is the moment when I used to help my mother preparing Pesto sauce.
We left Genoa and we emigrated to a small village on the Swiss border, when I was just a little girl.
Preparing Pesto, for my mother and my family was something like going back home.
That’s why it was so important for my mother to make it only when, coming back after visiting my grandparents and uncles based in Genoa, we could bring home, like a trophy, the original Genoese basil: Prà basil.
This basil has a particular sensory quality, that makes Pesto a very special sauce: tasty, genuine and, above all, healthy.
Its essential oils make it magic and you can easily recognize it from the scent, the color and the shape of the leaves. Remember, if you want to live this mystic experience: small, light green leaves in the shape of a teaspoon!
So even now, when I’m going to make homemade Pesto, I blindly follow my mother’s law: “Don’t make Pesto, if you can get Prà basil!”.
Furthermore, basil is not the only issue, when one talk about traditional Pesto sauce.
This sauce is a matter of legacy. Even if the modern recipe is not so ancient, it dates back to the beginning of the 20th century, it preserves the echoes of ancient recipes and know-hows coming especially from the Romans and from the Arabs.
It is the case for garlic, a disinfectant, and for coarse salt, known for its preservative properties. It is the case of pine nuts, strictly coming from Pisa, and of the two traditional cheese, Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Sardo. But, it’s also a matter of the know-how and backstory behind marble mortar and pestle, the traditional tools used since the origin of this and other Ligurian sauces.
In my opinion there is nothing so impressive and evocative as to get intensely inside the traditional cuisine of a place, in order to deeply grasp the meaning of its history and its evolutions.
But now let me bring you inside the family recipe and some tips that my mother passed on to me.
Seven are the ingredients and seven are the steps and the tips that I’m going to give you, let’s start!
1)	First step and first ingredient: garlic, possibly organic and Italian (top choice: Aglio from Vessalico). Peel it and remove the germ from the garlic clove and start to beat it inside the mortar;
2)	Add Pisa pine nuts (25/30 gr.) and keep beating them into a pulp.
3)	Put in 1 teaspoon of coarse salt and mix it.
4)	And now comes the moment of “his majesty” - basil: the leaves of one small bunch for each guest; this is one of the most crucial moments. As I told you before, basil boats very delicate and healthy essential oils and it’s extremely important to preserve them. So if you use the mortar and the pestle the movement should be precise and quick. If you are using a food processor, it’s vital, first of all,  to keep the  blender jar in the freezer for about an hour. It’s mandatory not to over heat the basil. So please be careful.
5)	Now you can add Parmigiano Reggiano (about 65/70 gr of 18/24 months aged cheese) freshly grated.
6)	And then you can add Pecorino Sardo (about 30/35 gr of 10 months cheese) freshly grated too.
7)	At the and of this process of melting and beating, another key moment: EVO, best if Ligurian. The quantity depends on the consistence we want to obtain that could be a little bit different according to the kind of pasta that you are going to dress. But it also crucial to add the oil scantily, without stopping to mix the sauce	
And that’s it, folks! Very soon Pesto sauce will be ready and your guests will be delighted and in love with it. 
And remember… it’s a family secret! ;-)
Ps.

images.title: Gnocchi al pesto - homemade.jpg
images.author: Fuerteadventours
images.description:
A matter of legacy: Pesto sauce.
One of the sweetest memories of my childhood, is the moment when I used to help my mother preparing Pesto sauce.
We left Genoa and we emigrated to a small village on the Swiss border, when I was just a little girl.
Preparing Pesto, for my mother and my family was something like going back home.
That’s why it was so important for my mother to make it only when, coming back after visiting my grandparents and uncles based in Genoa, we could bring home, like a trophy, the original Genoese basil: Prà basil.
This basil has a particular sensory quality, that makes Pesto a very special sauce: tasty, genuine and, above all, healthy.
Its essential oils make it magic and you can easily recognize it from the scent, the color and the shape of the leaves. Remember, if you want to live this mystic experience: small, light green leaves in the shape of a teaspoon!
So even now, when I’m going to make homemade Pesto, I blindly follow my mother’s law: “Don’t make Pesto, if you can get Prà basil!”.
Furthermore, basil is not the only issue, when one talk about traditional Pesto sauce.
This sauce is a matter of legacy. Even if the modern recipe is not so ancient, it dates back to the beginning of the 20th century, it preserves the echoes of ancient recipes and know-hows coming especially from the Romans and from the Arabs.
It is the case for garlic, a disinfectant, and for coarse salt, known for its preservative properties. It is the case of pine nuts, strictly coming from Pisa, and of the two traditional cheese, Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Sardo. But, it’s also a matter of the know-how and backstory behind marble mortar and pestle, the traditional tools used since the origin of this and other Ligurian sauces.
In my opinion there is nothing so impressive and evocative as to get intensely inside the traditional cuisine of a place, in order to deeply grasp the meaning of its history and its evolutions.
But now let me bring you inside the family recipe and some tips that my mother passed on to me.
Seven are the ingredients and seven are the steps and the tips that I’m going to give you, let’s start!
1)	First step and first ingredient: garlic, possibly organic and Italian (top choice: Aglio from Vessalico). Peel it and remove the germ from the garlic clove and start to beat it inside the mortar;
2)	Add Pisa pine nuts (25/30 gr.) and keep beating them into a pulp.
3)	Put in 1 teaspoon of coarse salt and mix it.
4)	And now comes the moment of “his majesty” - basil: the leaves of one small bunch for each guest; this is one of the most crucial moments. As I told you before, basil boats very delicate and healthy essential oils and it’s extremely important to preserve them. So if you use the mortar and the pestle the movement should be precise and quick. If you are using a food processor, it’s vital, first of all,  to keep the  blender jar in the freezer for about an hour. It’s mandatory not to over heat the basil. So please be careful.
5)	Now you can add Parmigiano Reggiano (about 65/70 gr of 18/24 months aged cheese) freshly grated.
6)	And then you can add Pecorino Sardo (about 30/35 gr of 10 months cheese) freshly grated too.
7)	At the and of this process of melting and beating, another key moment: EVO, best if Ligurian. The quantity depends on the consistence we want to obtain that could be a little bit different according to the kind of pasta that you are going to dress. But it also crucial to add the oil scantily, without stopping to mix the sauce	
And that’s it, folks! Very soon Pesto sauce will be ready and your guests will be delighted and in love with it. 
And remember… it’s a family secret! ;-)
Ps. 

leave a comment below, if you would like more information on the history of the pesto or on the recipes related to it

images.title: Oven Barbecued Beef Brisket.jpg
images.author: Home Cooking Secrets
images.description:
Are you in the mood for some Barbecue?? How about a nice Oven Barbecued Beef Brisket? Then you are in for a treat!
Oven Barbecued Beef Brisket Recipe.
Prep Time: 15 minutes
Bake Time: 3 hours
Ingredients:
1 - 3 to 3 1/2 pound beef brisket
2 cloves of garlic, minced
1 1/2 C bottled barbecue sauce (whatever is family favorite)
3/4 C water
1/2 C onion, finely diced
3 T Worcestershire sauce
2 T cider vinegar or white wine vinegar
1 T chili powder
1 tsp instant beef bouillon granules
1/8 tsp cayenne pepper
Preparation:
Trim fat from meat an place in a 13x9 baking dish.
In a small bowl mix together water, onion, Worcestershire sauce, vinegar, chili powder, bouillon granules, cayenne pepper and garlic. Pour over meat and cover with aluminum foil.
Place in oven preheated to 325*F for 3 hours or until tender, turning once half way through cooking time. Pour barbecue sauce over meat and return to oven to cook other half of time. Take from oven and let meat rest for 10 minutes. Remove meat from pan and thinly slice meat across the grain.
Per 2 1/2 ounces of beef with 2 tablespoons of the sauce poured over it : 244 calories, 7g total fat ( 2g sat. fat) 78 mg chol., 735 mg sodium, 13 g carbs, 29 g protein, 0 g fiber
Daily values: 8 % Vitamin A, 3 % Vitamin C, 2% Calcium, 17% iron
Exchanges: 1 "other" carbohydrate, 3 1/2 Lean Meat.
We hope you enjoyed this recipe and if you did, please be sure to share it with your friends and family and don't forget to click the 'Like' button for more delicious recipes, helpful tips and Home Cooking Secrets!

Watch how to make this Beef Brisket at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1MulZTZkdJ0

images.title: Nasi Iga Bakar - top - Warung Gudeg AUD9.50 (4673414361).jpg
images.author: Alpha from Melbourne, Australia
images.description:
There was a Nasi Iga Bakar on the the specials list. It'd be wrong not to try :)
After a bit of a wait, a good sign that it was freshly grilled, the result was three pieces of smoky charcoal grilled beef ribs sticky with sweet kicap manis and spice glaze. The burnt bits added a nice bitterness too!
If the ribs weren't good enough, accompanying it was a sambal chilli with slivers of zingy Kaffir Lime Leaves, great for adding a bit of freshness.

A fantastic little Indonesian place in the student heartland of Clayton.
Warung Gudeg
(03) 9558 6409
276 Clayton Rd
Clayton VIC 3168
